title: Hannah's silent prayer (1 Samuel 1)
hookLine: a childless woman prays with moving lips; the priest thinks she's drunk

cards: Every year a family travels up to Shiloh to bring an offering, and every year it goes the same way.
Elkanah gives portions of the meat to his wife Peninnah and her children, and a double portion to his other wife, Hannah, whom he loves. Hannah has no children.
And every year Peninnah provokes her about it, until Hannah weeps and won't eat. Her husband asks, kindly: am I not better to thee than ten sons? It doesn't reach her.
So after the meal she goes to the sanctuary and stands before God. An old priest named Eli is sitting by the doorpost, watching.

teach.b: What Eli sees is strange: a woman, her mouth moving, no sound coming out. "Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard." Eli decides she's drunk: how long will you be drunken?
The priest at the house of God looks at a woman praying with everything she has, and gets her completely wrong. She doesn't storm off, and she doesn't swallow it. She corrects him.
I am a woman of a sorrowful spirit; I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink, but "poured out my soul before the LORD." Don't count me as a worthless woman. Poured out, the way you'd empty a jar.
And Eli changes on the spot.

teach.h: HER FACE CHANGED BEFORE THE ANSWER.
teach.b: He doesn't defend himself. He says, "Go in peace," and adds a blessing: may the God of Israel grant what you asked. Then a line that's easy to miss.
Hannah goes her way, eats, and "her countenance was no more sad."
Nothing has happened yet, no child, only an old priest's blessing. The text doesn't explain the change; it records it, right after she has said it all to God.
The child comes later in the chapter, and she names him Samuel, saying she asked him of the Lord. It starts here, with a woman nobody could hear, and a priest who had to learn to listen.

how: Jews read Hannah's story as a model of personal prayer, and the Talmud draws from her the way the silent standing prayer, the Amidah, is said: lips moving, voice too low for others to hear.

o: the woman at Shiloh who prayed with lips moving, no sound
the rival wife who mocked another woman every year
the priest's wife who kept the lamp at Shiloh burning

games.q: hannah at shiloh — tap the pairs.
p: am I not better than ten sons?

s: Hannah prayed out loud and Eli overheard her
only her lips moved; her voice could not be heard. that's why Eli thought she was drunk.
Eli changed his mind and blessed her
he said go in peace, and asked that God grant her request.
Hannah's face stayed sad until her son was born
right after the prayer and Eli's blessing, her countenance was no more sad.

games.q: you're Hannah. you've just poured out your heart, and the priest accuses you of being drunk. what do you do?
o: answer him plainly: I'm not drunk, I poured out my soul.
argue that a priest should know better.
games.why: she answers him directly and without anger: no, my lord, I poured out my soul before the LORD. and Eli changes his mind and blesses her.

practice: Think of the thing you carry and rarely say out loud, the one that comes back every year like the trip to Shiloh, and let your lips move with it, your voice too low to hear.
If you pray, pour it out to God the way Hannah did; if you don't, just let it be said, all of it, once.

wordCard.voice: Hannah. The woman at Shiloh whose lips moved without sound, mistaken for drunk, who answered the priest and poured out her soul.

carryVoice: Your line: she spoke in her heart. Eli heard her once he stopped judging. Day seven hundred twenty-seven.
